extracted.intended_audience: poets, rhetoricians, and students of poetics / creative-writing practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing poetic diction and narrative (epic & tragic): how to choose words, metaphors, metre, and plot-unity so language is clear yet elevated and plots are probable and organically unified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfection of diction: clear and not mean
rubrics_metrics.description: The perfection of diction is for it to be at once clear and not mean.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ordinary words for clearness and unfamiliar/ornamental terms for distinction; mix these elements so the language is neither prosaic nor obscure. Avoid making whole statements of strange words (barbarism) or of metaphors alone (riddle). Test diction by substituting ordinary words to see the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of metaphor — mastery and moderation
rubrics_metrics.description: The greatest thing by far is to be a master of metaphor; a good metaphor implies an intuitive perception of the similarity in dissimilars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metaphor is a mark of genius and cannot be learned wholly from others. Use metaphors to achieve distinction, but apply the rule of moderation — improper or excessive metaphors produce ludicrous or riddle-like effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strange words, coined words, and ornamental forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Strange words and coined words give diction a non-prosaic character but, if used throughout, become barbarisms or riddles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ strange/lengthened/curtailed/altered forms and compounds selectively to render diction non-prosaic while preserving clarity. Avoid overuse that leads to ludicrous effects; different genres tolerate different amounts (see genre-appropriate diction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of moderation in poetic vocabulary
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule of moderation applies to all the constituents of the poetic vocabulary; a too apparent use of licences has a ludicrous effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not over-use metaphors, strange words, or ornamental equivalents. Where action, character, or thought are present, over-ornate diction tends to obscure them; elaborate diction is mainly needed where no action or character is revealed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre-appropriate diction (which forms fit which genre)
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the kinds of words enumerated, compounds are most in place in the dithyramb, strange words in heroic, and metaphors in iambic poetry; heroic poetry may avail itself of them all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match diction to the genre: heroic metre tolerates more strange words/metaphors; iambic models spoken language and should stick to ordinary words, metaphor, and ornamental equivalents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic plot unity — single action and organic completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: The construction of its stories should be based on a single action, one that is a complete whole in itself, with a beginning, middle, and end, so as to enable the work to produce its own proper pleasure with all the organic unity of a living creature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a coherent section of a larger tradition if necessary (Homer's practice). Episodes are permissible to relieve uniformity but should not break the single-action unity; avoid treating an entire vast sequence as one epic action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between history and epic
rubrics_metrics.description: A history deals not with one action, but with one period and all that happened in that to one or more persons, however disconnected the several events may have been.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not mistake episodic or period-spanning narrative for epic unity; epic should aim at an organic single-action structure rather than a catalog of disconnected events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic species and constituent parts (parallels to tragedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic poetry must divide into the same species as tragedy; it must be either simple or complex, a story of character or one of suffering, and requires peripeties, discoveries, and scenes of suffering like tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure epic contains the dramatic elements (peripety, discovery, suffering) as appropriate; thought and diction must be good 'in their way' to satisfy the epic form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic length and metre appropriateness
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic length must permit the beginning and end to be taken in one view; heroic metre is the gravest and weightiest, appropriate to narrative, and epic should not be written in a medley of metres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the poem roughly as long as a series of tragedies offered for one hearing; use heroic metre for long narrative — mixing metres is incongruous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial presence — minimal propria persona
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should say very little propria persona, as he is no imitator when doing that; Homer after a brief preface brings in forthwith a man, a woman, or some other character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minimize overt authorial intrusion; let characters and action carry the imitation. Excessive first-person authorial commentary reduces the imitative/poetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marvellous and improbability: placement and concealment
rubrics_metrics.description: The marvellous is required in tragedy; the epic affords more opening for the improbable. A likely impossibility is always preferable to an unconvincing possibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If improbable incidents are unavoidable, place them outside the piece (e.g., ignorance of background) rather than within the action. Conceal improbabilities by other excellences; where improbabilities could be avoided without loss, they are faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of technical or factual errors
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two kinds of error — one directly connected with the art (fault in expression/power) and one accidentally connected with it (technical/scientific mistakes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the error arises from failure of poetic expression, it is the art's fault; if the poet deliberately misdescribes for poetic ends (e.g., drawing men 'as they ought to be'), the error is not in the essentials of poetic art. Prefer technical correctness where it does not impair poetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objections critics raise (five kinds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics' objections usually allege that something is either (1) impossible, (2) improbable, (3) corrupting, (4) contradictory, or (5) against technical correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respond by: (1) justifying impossibility by poetic requirements or opinion; (2) justifying improbability by opinion or occurrence against probability; (3) testing contradictions dialectically for alternative senses; (4) treating corrupting material in context of agent/motive/time; and (5) noting whether a technical mistake is accidental or inexcusable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublimity: definition and primary effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Sublimity is a certain distinction and excellence in expression; its effect upon an audience is not persuasion, but transport — it brings power and irresistible might to bear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for transportive elevated language that elicits rapt attention; sublimity is an immediate emotional and intellectual elevation rather than mere logical persuasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art and nature in achieving the sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: Some elements of sublimity are innate (nature) but system (art) can define fitting limits and seasons; nature supplies impulse, art supplies curb and practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate natural gifts through disciplined practice and rules; do not leave sublime expression unstable or unballasted — combine inspiration with knowledge and technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid tumidity (overblown bombast)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tumidity is turbid expression and confused imagery rather than true intensity; overblown phrases sink from the terrible into the contemptible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject tasteless swelling, inflated metaphors, and bombastic phrasing (e.g., trivial or grotesque grandiose epithets). Elevation must be genuine, not mere ornament; test by whether the line survives daylight scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid puerility / frigidity (pedantic triviality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Puerility (frigidity) is the direct antithesis of elevation — pedant's thoughts that begin in learned trifling and end in frigidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid affected, childish or merely clever imagery that undermines dignity. Examples include strained comparisons and trivial conceits that call attention to the writer's cleverness rather than elevating the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid parenthyrsus (unseasonable or immoderate passion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parenthyrsus is unseasonable and empty passion where no passion is required, or immoderate passion where moderation is needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place passion only where the subject demands it; avoid personal, intoxicated displays of emotion that the audience cannot share — ensure emotion is organically motivated by the material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance novelty with stability — novelty's dangers
rubrics_metrics.description: The pursuit of novelty in expression often produces defects; beauties of expression can be the elements of their own contrary faults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use novel turns of phrase sparingly and for effect; be aware that variation, hyperbole, and plural usages that seem attractive can lead to tumidity, puerility, or frigidity if misapplied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for genuine sublimity (tests of greatness)
rubrics_metrics.description: True sublimity pleases all and always, survives repeated hearing, disposes the soul to high thoughts, leaves food for reflection, and is hard to efface from the memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge passages by their enduring effect across diverse audiences and repeated readings; if the 'elevation' collapses under analysis or fails to inspire high thoughts, it is not genuine sublimity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means to attain sublimity (practice and knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: The best means are to gain clear knowledge and appreciation of the true sublime; judgment of style is the fruit of long experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate discrimination through study and practice; use rules as aids to channel nature, and learn from exemplars while seeking the capacity to induce transport in readers.
